---
title: "Reading a CFR citation"
order: 1
---

## The ticket

A Quality Analyst at Lakeshore Blood Center forwards you a deviation report. A unit of red
blood cells sat at the wrong storage temperature for four hours before someone caught it on a
chart review. The write-up ends with one line: "Corrective action: retrain staff on 606.160."

You supervise this person. Your CIO is going to ask you what happened. Before you can answer
either of them, you need to know what "606.160" actually is, what it requires, and whether
retraining is even the right fix — or whether it's a fig leaf over a records gap that's about
to become a bigger problem.

Right now you can't tell. That's the gap this lesson closes.

## Why this rule exists

Blood banking runs on paper and screens, not just refrigerators. A unit of blood is only as
trustworthy as the trail behind it: who drew it, what it tested for, what temperature it lived
at, who released it, who received it. If that trail has a hole, nobody — not Lakeshore, not
FDA, not the hospital that transfused the unit — can answer the question that matters after
something goes wrong: *was this unit safe, and how do we know?*

FDA's answer is a records requirement with teeth: 21 CFR 606.160. It doesn't just say "keep
good records." It enumerates categories of records a blood establishment must maintain —
donor records, processing records, storage and distribution records, compatibility test
records, quality control records — and sets rules for how long to keep them and what they have
to contain.

In ITSM terms, this is your **configuration management database (CMDB) and audit trail
requirements, written into federal law, for a product that goes into a human body.** You
already know why a CMDB with gaps is dangerous — you can't run change enablement, root cause
analysis, or an incident postmortem against records that don't exist or don't match reality.
Same failure mode here, except the "asset" is a unit of blood, the "incident" is a patient
reaction, and the auditor isn't your compliance team — it's an FDA investigator with statutory
authority to shut down manufacturing.

## The rule, in plain English

606.160 says a blood establishment has to keep specific records for specific things, in real
time, and keep them long enough to be useful if something goes wrong later. Four ideas do most
of the work:

- **Record concurrently, not retroactively.** You document a step *as* it happens, not from
  memory afterward.
- **Cover the whole chain.** Donor screening, collection, processing, storage, distribution,
  and compatibility testing each get their own record categories — not one generic log.
- **Make records complete enough to reconstruct history.** Who did the work, when, what the
  result was, and how it was interpreted — not just a checkbox that it happened.
- **Keep them long enough to matter.** Retention is tied to the product's expiration date, not
  a fixed calendar rule, because the question "was this unit safe" can surface months after the
  unit is gone.

At Lakeshore, that means the four-hour temperature excursion isn't just an unfortunate lapse —
it's a gap in a *storage record* that 606.160(b)(3) specifically requires the center to
maintain. The deviation report itself, once written and retained, becomes part of the record
trail the rule demands. "Retrain staff" doesn't touch that. More on this in the traps section.

## Citation decoder

This is the first CFR citation in the curriculum, so before decoding 606.160 itself, here's how
the whole numbering system is built — top to bottom, broadest to narrowest.

| Level | Value here | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Title | 21 | One of 50 subject-matter titles in the CFR. Title 21 is Food and Drugs — it covers FDA's entire regulatory turf, from food labeling to medical devices to blood. |
| Chapter | I | A major subdivision of the title, assigned to one agency. Chapter I is FDA. |
| Subchapter | F | A grouping of related parts within the chapter. Subchapter F is Biologics. |
| Part | 606 | A specific regulatory program. Part 606 is Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) for Blood and Blood Components — the rules for *how* blood gets collected and processed, not just what's allowed. |
| Subpart | D | A thematic grouping within the part. Subpart D is Records and Reports. |
| Section | 606.160 | The actual rule. Section numbers restart within each part, so "606.160" only means something in combination with "Part 606" — that's why the full citation always includes the part number as the first three digits. |
| Paragraph | (b)(1) | A specific clause inside the section. Paragraphs nest: (b) is a top-level paragraph, (1) is a numbered subparagraph inside it, and you'll see a third level like (b)(1)(viii) go one deeper still, using lowercase roman numerals. |

Two things worth locking in now, because every later lesson assumes them:

**"Part" and "section" are not interchangeable**, even though people say both loosely.
"Part 606" is the whole CGMP program — dozens of sections. "Section 606.160" is one rule inside
it. When someone says "we're out of compliance with Part 606," ask which section — that's the
difference between a program-level statement and an actionable finding.

**Reading a full citation aloud:** "606.160(b)(1)" is read as "six-oh-six point one-six-oh,
paragraph b, subparagraph one" — or more naturally in conversation, "section 606.160,
paragraph (b)(1)." You don't need to recite "Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter F" out loud in
normal use; those are for locating the rule in the code, not for talking about it day to day.
Inspectors and Quality Analysts alike just say "606.160(b)(1)."

Here's the decoder applied to two specific clauses this lesson uses:

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(3) | "Six-oh-six point one-six-oh, paragraph b, sub-three" | Storage and distribution records, including storage temperature with initialed temperature recorder charts | The four-hour excursion has to show up in the unit's storage record, temperature-charted and initialed — not just described in a deviation narrative |
| 21 CFR 606.160(d) | "Six-oh-six point one-six-oh, paragraph d" | Retention: individual product records kept at least 10 years after processing, or 6 months past the latest expiration date, whichever is later | Whatever record gets generated from this deviation has a retention clock attached to it, not a "keep it a while" expectation |

## The actual text

Quoting 606.160(b)(3) verbatim, from the storage and distribution records list (source:
`sources/cfr/606.160.md`, retrieved from eCFR):

> (3) Storage and distribution records:
>
> (i) Distribution and disposition, as appropriate, of blood and blood products.
>
> (ii) Visual inspection of whole blood and red blood cells during storage and immediately
> before distribution.
>
> (iii) Storage temperature, including initialed temperature recorder charts.
>
> (iv) Reissue, including records of proper temperature maintenance.
>
> (v) Emergency release of blood, including signature of requesting physician obtained before
> or after release.

Clause (iii) is the one that bites Lakeshore directly: "storage temperature, including
initialed temperature recorder charts" is not optional documentation — it's a named record
category. If the four-hour excursion isn't reflected in an initialed chart, the *record itself*
is deficient, independent of whatever caused the temperature problem in the first place.

And the retention clause, 606.160(d), in the regulation's own words:

> Records shall be retained for such interval beyond the expiration date for the blood or blood
> component as necessary to facilitate the reporting of any unfavorable clinical reactions. You
> must retain individual product records no less than 10 years after the records of processing
> are completed or 6 months after the latest expiration date for the individual product,
> whichever is the later date.

Note the word choice: "shall" and "must" both appear here. Both are regulatory language in this
section — FDA uses "must" in some CFR provisions (typically ones written or revised more
recently, in plain-language style) and "shall" in others, but within Part 606 both carry
binding force. That's different from FDA *guidance* documents, which use "should" — a signal
this lesson's traps section comes back to.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator doesn't ask "do you have a records policy." They ask for the record. For
this scenario, that means: pull the storage temperature chart for the affected unit, show it
initialed, show the time span, and show what happened when the temperature went out of range.

The document that proves compliance here is the **temperature recorder chart plus the
deviation record**, not the training log. Ownership sits with whoever runs blood storage
operations — a lab or quality operations lead, with the Quality Analyst responsible for the
deviation file and its CAPA (corrective and preventive action — the quality-system term for
"fix the immediate problem, then fix the process that let it happen," CAPA gets its own lesson
later in the curriculum).

A bad answer sounds like: "we retrained staff, so it won't happen again." That answers
*why* the excursion happened, maybe. It says nothing about whether the record itself now meets
606.160(b)(3) — was the chart initialed, is the deviation traceable to the specific unit, is
retention now attached per 606.160(d). An inspector who hears "we retrained staff" as the whole
answer will ask to see the chart next. If it's missing or incomplete, the finding isn't "staff
made an error" — it's "the records system has a gap," which is a much worse finding because it
implies every other unit's chart might have the same problem.

## Common traps

**"Part 606 is 'the blood regulation,' so any blood rule is 606.something."** Not true. Donor
eligibility and testing requirements live largely in Part 630 and Part 610 — you'll see
610.40 and 630.40 cited inside 606.160 itself, cross-referencing those parts. Part 606 is
specifically about *manufacturing practice* — the CGMP program. A citation to "606" doesn't
tell you the topic; you need the section.

**"If it's on FDA's website and sounds authoritative, it's a regulation."** FDA publishes
guidance documents constantly — recommendations on how to comply, written in "should" language,
that are not themselves binding law. CFR text is regulation: enacted through formal rulemaking,
binding, cited with a Title-Part-Section-Paragraph reference like the one in this lesson, using
"shall" or "must." Guidance documents explain FDA's current thinking on how to meet a
regulation, are cited by document title and date, and use "should." A third category — AABB
Standards — is a private accreditation body's requirements, binding only if Lakeshore holds
AABB accreditation, and cited by standard number, never quoted verbatim here since AABB
Standards text is copyrighted. Confusing these three is one of the fastest ways to lose
credibility with an inspector or in a written response to a 483 (FDA's form for documenting
inspectional observations) — citing a guidance document as if it were a regulatory requirement,
or vice versa, reads as not understanding the difference. The next foundation lesson,
`regulatory-landscape-orientation`, is built entirely around telling these apart.

## What this means for your job

- **Don't accept "we fixed the process" as a closed deviation until you've seen the record it
  produced.** The corrective action and the record are two different deliverables — a training
  session doesn't repair a missing chart entry.
- **When a Quality Analyst cites a section number to you, ask them to say the paragraph too.**
  "606.160" alone is a pointer to a page with a dozen sub-requirements. "606.160(b)(3)" tells
  you exactly what's at issue. If they can't give you the paragraph, they may not have actually
  looked at the text.
- **Retention isn't a records-management afterthought — it's a regulatory clock.** Any system
  or vendor decision that touches blood product records (a new BECS platform, a document
  archive migration, a retention policy change) has to respect 606.160(d)'s 10-year-or-6-months
  math, not your organization's generic IT retention schedule.
- **Distinguish "shall/must" from "should" the moment someone cites something to you.** If a
  recommendation comes to you as a hard requirement, ask what it's actually citing — a CFR
  section, a guidance document, or an AABB standard. The escalation path and the risk exposure
  are different for each.
- **A records gap is a worse finding than a records error.** An investigator who finds one bad
  temperature chart has a data point. One who finds that your process doesn't reliably produce
  a chart at all has a systemic finding — and systemic findings are what turn into consent
  decrees, not just 483 observations.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: A colleague says "we're covered under Part 606 for our temperature logging." Is that specific enough to know your obligation?

No. Part 606 covers all of blood CGMP — donor deferral cross-references, general provisions,
records, reports, and more. Temperature logging specifically falls under 606.160(b)(3),
inside the Records subpart. "Part 606" tells you the general topic area; only the section (and
usually the paragraph) tells you the actual requirement. Always ask for the section number.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The Quality Analyst says "FDA guidance requires 10-year record retention for blood products." Is that accurate?

Not as stated. The 10-year-or-6-months-past-expiration retention rule comes from 21 CFR
606.160(d) — that's a *regulation*, not guidance. The word "guidance" here is being used
loosely to mean "FDA rule," which is exactly the kind of imprecision that causes problems in an
inspection response. Correcting this distinction, and knowing when something really is
guidance rather than regulation, is worth catching every time — it's the subject of the next
foundation lesson.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A unit's temperature chart is missing an initial next to one entry, but the temperature value itself was correct and in range. Does 606.160(b)(3) still apply?

Yes. 606.160(b)(3)(iii) requires "storage temperature, including initialed temperature
recorder charts" — the initial is part of the record requirement, not decoration. A correct
temperature value on an unsigned chart doesn't satisfy the rule; the record has to show who
attested to it. This is a smaller finding than a missing chart entirely, but it's still a
finding, and it's the kind of gap a records audit is built to catch.
:::

## Where this goes next

You can now take apart any CFR citation you'll see in this curriculum and know what each piece
means. The next foundation, `regulatory-landscape-orientation`, builds directly on the traps
section above: given any rule — a CFR section, an FDA guidance document, an AABB standard, or
just "how we've always done it" — you'll be able to say which category it's in and which one
actually binds Lakeshore.
